title: 3Sum — sort + two-pointer for remaining pair.
shortTitle: 3Sum — Sort Then Two-Pointer for the Remaining Pair

s1_definition.profdef: The 3Sum problem finds all unique triplets in an array that sum to zero (or a target). The efficient approach sorts the array, then fixes one element and uses opposite-end two pointers on the remaining subarray to find pairs that complete the triplet. Duplicate triplets are skipped by advancing past repeated values. It runs in O(n squared) time and O(1) extra space beyond the sort.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to find every set of three adjustments that net to zero so they cancel out. Rajesh sorts the adjustments, then fixes the first one and uses two fingers from the ends of the rest to find a matching pair that brings the total to zero, skipping repeats so he never reports the same trio twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort first, fix one element, then run opposite-end two pointers on the rest — skipping duplicates — to collect all triplets in O(n squared).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The 3Sum problem finds all unique triplets in an array that sum to zero (or a target). The efficient approach sorts the array, then fixes one element and uses opposite-end two pointers on the remaining subarray to find pairs that complete the triplet. Duplicate triplets are skipped by advancing past repeated values. It runs in O(n squared) time and O(1) extra space beyond the sort.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to find every set of three adjustments that net to zero so they cancel out. Rajesh sorts the adjustments, then fixes the first one and uses two fingers from the ends of the rest to find a matching pair that brings the total to zero, skipping repeats so he never reports the same trio twice.

**One line to remember:** Sort first, fix one element, then run opposite-end two pointers on the rest — skipping duplicates — to collect all triplets in O(n squared).

sections.s2_technical:
First sort the array; this enables both the two-pointer pair search and easy duplicate skipping. Then loop with an index `i` from 0 to n-3, fixing `a[i]` as the first element of the triplet. If `a[i]` is greater than the target and all values are non-negative after sorting you can break early, a common optimization.

For each fixed `i`, set `left = i + 1` and `right = n - 1`. Compute `sum = a[i] + a[left] + a[right]`. If the sum equals the target, record the triplet, then move both pointers inward while skipping duplicates: `while (left < right && a[left] == a[left+1]) left++;` and similarly for `right`. If the sum is less than the target move `left` up; if greater move `right` down.

A code snippet: `for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) { if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i-1]) continue; int l = i+1, r = n-1; while (l < r) { int s = a[i]+a[l]+a[r]; if (s == 0) { result.add(List.of(a[i],a[l],a[r])); while (l<r && a[l]==a[l+1]) l++; while (l<r && a[r]==a[r-1]) r--; l++; r--; } else if (s < 0) l++; else r--; } }`. The `continue` on `i` skips duplicate first elements.

A senior nuance is the three places duplicates must be skipped: the fixed element `i`, the left pointer after a match, and the right pointer after a match. Missing any produces duplicate triplets. The overall complexity is O(n squared) because the sort is O(n log n) and the fixed-element loop with the inner two-pointer scan is O(n squared), which dominates. This is a classic example of reducing a naive O(n cubed) triple loop to O(n squared) using sorting plus two pointers.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a month-end netting process where ledger adjustments can be positive or negative, and the risk team wants every unique group of three adjustments that cancel to zero so they can be closed together. This is exactly how 3Sum works — sort the adjustments and find all zero-summing triplets.

Problem 2 — The same cancelling trio must never be reported twice even if duplicate adjustment amounts exist, which is why duplicate skipping is essential.

The code shows a `NettingService` with `findZeroTriplets`, a demo on a list of signed adjustments, and the unique triplets found.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: adjustments [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2, 2]. After sorting it is already [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2, 2].

Step 1: `i` is 0 fixing -4. `left` at -1 (index 1), `right` at 2 (index 6). Sum is -4 minus 1 plus 2 equals -3, less than zero, so `left` moves up. It keeps moving because the sum stays negative until `left` passes `right`, so -4 yields no triplet.

Step 2: `i` is 1 fixing -1. `left` at index 2 (-1), `right` at index 6 (2). Sum is -1 minus 1 plus 2 equals 0, a match, so we record [-1, -1, 2]. We then skip the duplicate 2 at `right` and move both inward.

Step 3: Now `left` at index 3 (0), `right` at index 4 (1). Sum is -1 plus 0 plus 1 equals 0, another match, so we record [-1, 0, 1]. Pointers move inward and cross, ending this fixed element.

Step 4: `i` is 2 fixing -1 again, but since it equals the previous `a[i-1]` it is skipped to avoid duplicate triplets. `i` is 3 fixing 0; `left` and `right` search but no zero-sum pair is found.

Step 5: `i` is 4 fixing 1, which is greater than 0, so the early break stops the loop. The result is the two unique triplets [-1, -1, 2] and [-1, 0, 1].

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Found 2 unique triplets
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Zero-summing triplets: [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [-4,-1,-1,0,1,2,2] (sorted)
    │
    ▼
  i=0(-4): sums stay <0 → no triplet
  i=1(-1): l=-1 r=2 sum=0 → record [-1,-1,2], skip dup
           l=0  r=1 sum=0 → record [-1,0,1]
  i=2(-1): duplicate of i=1 → skip
  i=3(0):  no pair sums to 0
  i=4(1):  a[i]>0 → break
    ▼
  Result: [[-1,-1,2], [-1,0,1]]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The 3Sum problem asks me to find every unique triplet in an array that sums to zero, and the efficient approach combines sorting with two pointers. I first sort the array, which lets me both run an opposite-end pointer search and skip duplicates cleanly. Then I fix each element as the first member of the triplet, and for the remaining part of the array I place a left pointer just after the fixed element and a right pointer at the end, moving them inward based on whether the current three-way sum is below, above, or equal to zero.

The detail that separates a correct answer from a buggy one is duplicate handling in three distinct places. I skip a fixed element if it equals the previous fixed element, and after recording a matching triplet I advance the left pointer past any repeated value and retreat the right pointer past any repeated value before moving both inward. Missing any of these three skips produces the same triplet more than once, which is the most common mistake on this problem.

On complexity, sorting is order n log n, and the fixed-element loop wrapping the linear two-pointer scan is order n squared, which dominates, so the whole thing is quadratic with constant extra space beyond the sort. That is a big improvement over the naive triple loop which is cubic.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the month-end netting service. Ledger adjustments could be positive or negative, and the risk team wanted every unique group of three adjustments that cancelled to zero so they could be closed together, and because duplicate adjustment amounts were common the duplicate-skipping logic ensured no cancelling trio was ever reported twice. Explaining the sort, the fix-one-plus-two-pointer structure, and especially the three duplicate-skip points shows the interviewer I understand both the algorithm and the correctness pitfalls.
